query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: At temperatures above roughly 1500 K, the nanoparticles’ high thermal energy increases atomic diffusion such that in a reactive (catalytic) ambient, selective oxidation or gas interactions lower the local bonding stability, triggering surface segregation and incipient phase separation, whereas in an inert (thermoelectric) atmosphere the high configurational entropy and lattice distortion effectively maintain the homogeneous solid-solution structure.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in near‐equiatomic ratios, crystallized as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with minimal initial chemical ordering.
generation.intervention: Controlled temperature ramping from 473 K to 1923 K while alternating between reactive (e.g., oxygen-containing) and inert (e.g., argon) gas environments.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted over the full temperature range using in situ high-temperature XRD combined with TEM/EDS to monitor phase and chemical evolution; the test applies when the metal constituents have moderate size differences (within Hume–Rothery limits) so that lattice distortion plays a stabilizing role.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of lattice distortion augmented by oxidation-induced weakening of interatomic bonding in reactive environments.
generation.mechanism: In reactive conditions, high temperatures enhance atomic diffusion and, together with gas-phase interactions, lower the effective diffusion barriers for certain elements. This promotes selective oxidation and local chemical ordering or segregation, destabilizing the solid solution. In contrast, inert conditions suppress oxidation so that the high configurational entropy combined with lattice distortion preserves the uniform solid-solution phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under catalytic (reactive) conditions, in situ XRD and TEM/EDS will reveal signs of surface segregation, formation of minor secondary phases, or local chemical ordering (especially at temperatures above ~1500 K). Conversely, under inert (thermoelectric) conditions, the nanoparticles will retain their single-phase structure with only minor lattice distortions.
generation.baseline: Initial characterization at room temperature shows a uniform, crystallized single-phase solid solution with homogeneously distributed elements.
generation.boundary: The prediction holds provided that the nanoparticles’ metal constituents conform to moderate atomic size disparities (e.g., within 15% as per Hume–Rothery guidelines) and are not subject to extreme gas reactivity that would overwhelm diffusion effects. Very small nanoparticles or strong support interactions might modulate the observed effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature threshold for segregation onset and the quantitative extent of chemical ordering depend on the specific metal combination and nanoparticle size. Additionally, the relative impacts of oxidation versus thermal diffusion require further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Subject identical nanoparticle samples to a controlled temperature ramp from 473 K to 1923 K while alternating the ambient gas between a reactive (oxygen-containing) and an inert (argon) atmosphere. In situ XRD will track phase changes, while TEM/EDS will provide elemental mapping and detect evidence of segregation or secondary phase formation.
measurements: Phase identification and lattice parameter shifts from in situ high-temperature XRD
Elemental mapping and detection of chemical inhomogeneity via TEM/EDS
Surface oxidation states measured by XPS (if applicable)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across the tested temperature range, no significant difference is observed between the reactive and inert environments—in particular, if no evidence of surface segregation, chemical ordering, or emergent secondary phases is detected under reactive conditions compared to inert ones—the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

This implies that there could be an upper bound on the extent of atomic size dispersion allowable in HEAs. The relevance of this rule to HEAs is an open question deserving further investigation; for example, see Ref. (). We demonstrate that temperature and lattice distortion jointly contribute to numerous thermodynamic, structural, and elastic properties via a unified effective temperature, encompassing both the actual temperature and the extent of lattice distortion. Lattice distortion notably enhances the stability of a single-phase solid solution, as commonly found in binary and multicomponent alloys, by elevating the effective temperature. Increasing temperature further reinforces the stability of a solid solution compared to phase separation or ordering. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are solid solutions consisting of five or more metallic elements in approximately equimolar ratios with elemental compositions typically between 5–35 atomic percent (at.%). They have attracted increasing attention, especially as structural materials, due to their remarkable mechanical strength and resistance to oxidation and fatigue at ambient and elevated temperatures. The compositional complexity does not automatically imply microstructural complexity due to the high mixing entropy. Often, an operational definition for HEAs is a solid-solution phase stabilized by the higher configurational entropy that increases with increasing temperature. With increasing the number of alloying elements (N), it should be noted, however, that the entropy increases as N ln N whereas interacting pairs that may drive chemical order increase as N2; so at low temperatures any favorable ordering enthalpy could overcome the slower increasing entropy – a point often not given its due importance.
